interview_metadata.name: Osvaldo Vargas
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Sure, happy to. I was born in Queens, New York in 1986. My parents had come up from Guayaquil, Ecuador in the early eighties — my dad worked in a commercial bakery and my mom cleaned office buildings at night and did alterations from home during the day. Spanish was the only language in the house until I started kindergarten, and even then we kept it Spanish at the dinner table. We moved to Milwaukee when I was about ten because my dad's cousin had a line on a maintenance job at a hospital there, and the rent was a fraction of New York. I went to public school in the city, got pulled into a math and science magnet program in seventh grade, and that's really where I got hooked on building things — we did a bridge-loading competition with popsicle sticks and I was the kid who stayed after to redesign the gusset plates. I did my undergrad at UW-Milwaukee, civil engineering, graduated in 2009 right into the recession, which was rough — I waited tables and did drafting contract work for almost two years before I got on with a mid-sized firm doing municipal projects. I met my wife Camila at a Habitat for Humanity build in 2012; she's a pediatric speech-language pathologist. We got married in 2015, bought our house in Menomonee Falls in 2018, and our daughter Lucia was born in 2019, right before everything shut down. We lost my dad to a stroke in 2021, which is still the hardest thing I've been through. Work-wise I've been at the same firm for nine years now, just made senior associate, and I'm grinding through the PE exam prep. That's the broad strokes.

follow_ups.question: What was the move from Queens to Milwaukee like for a ten-year-old?
follow_ups.response: Honestly disorienting. Queens was loud, dense, everyone in our building was Ecuadorian or Dominican or Colombian. Milwaukee felt empty and cold and very white, and the first winter I genuinely thought my mom had made a terrible mistake. But I made friends through soccer pretty fast — that was the bridge.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned losing your dad in 2021. How has that shaped you?
follow_ups.response: It rearranged my priorities, frankly. He worked himself ragged so I could sit in an office and design bridges, and I think about that a lot. I call my mom every Sunday now without fail. And I started taking my vacation days — he never did, and I'm not going to repeat that.

follow_ups.question: How did meeting Camila at the Habitat build change things for you?
follow_ups.response: She was framing a wall and roasting one of the site leads for using a level wrong, and I just thought, okay, this is the person. We dated for about three years before we got married. She grounds me — I'm the one who'll say yes to four committees, and she's the one who'll say, 'Osvaldo, when are you sleeping?'

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, my big crossroads was in 2010. I'd been out of school for over a year, working at a chain restaurant on Brady Street and picking up CAD work where I could, and a recruiter for an oil and gas firm in Houston called me. Real money — almost double what any Milwaukee firm was offering. My mom wanted me to take it; she'd been carrying me on her insurance and she was tired. I drove down to Houston for an interview, stayed with a college buddy, and the project they wanted me on was a pipeline corridor through a residential area where the community meetings had basically been a formality. I came back, sat with it for a week, and turned it down. I took a junior position at my current firm at almost half the salary and lived in my parents' basement for another eighteen months. That decision is why I do the work I do now — community-facing infrastructure, public art integration, the whole thing. If I'd gone to Houston I'd probably have a bigger house and a much smaller sense of myself.

follow_ups.question: What did your mom say when you turned it down?
follow_ups.response: She cried, honestly. Not angry — just tired. She came around once she saw I was serious about the path. By the time I got my first real raise she was bragging about me at church.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever second-guess that decision?
follow_ups.response: Almost never. Maybe once during the pandemic when daycare was closed and we were burning through savings, I thought about what that Houston salary would've looked like compounded over a decade. But no, it was the right call.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was very conscious. I made a pros and cons list, I called my undergrad advisor, I prayed about it, I talked to my pastor at the time. I wanted to be sure I wasn't romanticizing being broke. It was a deliberate choice with my eyes open.

follow_ups.question: Is that typical of how you make big decisions?
follow_ups.response: Pretty much. I'm an engineer — I build a spreadsheet for almost everything. Camila teases me about it.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly, the Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers chapter at UWM helped a lot — they had alumni who'd been through similar choices and were willing to talk. A formal mentorship program tied to the regional firms would've shortened my unemployed stretch by a year, easy.

follow_ups.question: Do you mentor others now because of that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very intentionally. I take on at least two SHPE student mentees a year and I always answer the cold LinkedIn messages from Latino engineering students.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: Yes — my wife Camila, who's 37, and our daughter Lucia, who just turned six in March. Camila is from Mexico City originally; her family came here when she was twelve, so we both have that immigrant-kid shorthand. She works at a pediatric clinic in Wauwatosa doing speech-language pathology, mostly with kids on the autism spectrum. Lucia is in kindergarten at the elementary school right behind our subdivision and is obsessed with dinosaurs and Encanto. My mom, Gloria, is 68 and lives in a condo in West Allis — she retired from cleaning last year and now does some sewing work on the side because she can't sit still. My sister Marisol is two years younger than me, she's a nurse anesthetist in Madison, married to a guy named Trevor who's a high school history teacher; they have twin boys who are four. My dad's side of the family is mostly still in Guayaquil — my tío Hector and tía Rosa and a swarm of cousins. We FaceTime with them most Sundays.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your mom in person?
follow_ups.response: At least every other weekend. She comes for Sunday lunch most weeks — Camila and I take turns hosting with Marisol. And she stays with us for a week every February when Camila and I take a winter trip.

follow_ups.question: What's your relationship with your sister like?
follow_ups.response: Tight. She's my best friend, honestly. We text every day, mostly memes and complaining about our kids. She's the only person who can tell me to slow down and I'll actually listen.

follow_ups.question: How often do you make it down to Ecuador?
follow_ups.response: Not often enough. We went in 2017, before Lucia, and I really want to take her before she turns ten. We've been saying 'next year' since the pandemic.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Camila's parents are in Pewaukee, about twenty minutes from us. We're close — they take Lucia every other Friday evening so we can get a date night. Her dad Rafael and I watch the Bucks together.

follow_ups.question: Any siblings on Camila's side?
follow_ups.response: She has one younger brother, Andrés, who lives in Denver. We see him at Christmas mostly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: A few. My soccer crew — about eight of us who've been playing together in the co-ed league for six or seven years. Diego and Marcus especially; we grab beers after games at Sprecher's Tap Room. Then there's Priya, a structural engineer at my firm who I came up with — she's my go-to sounding board for office politics. And my friend Jamal from the Habitat board; he's a community organizer with MICAH and we've worked on a couple of advocacy projects together. Father Esteban at St. Mary's is also important to me, even though I don't go to mass every week — he was a huge support when my dad died.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see the soccer crew outside of games?
follow_ups.response: We have a group chat that's constantly going. We do a poker night every couple of months and there's an annual ice fishing trip up to Eagle River in February.

follow_ups.question: What does Priya mean to your career?
follow_ups.response: She's the one who pushed me to ask for senior associate when I was going to wait another year. She negotiates harder than I do, and watching her do it has made me better at it.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We're in a subdivision in Menomonee Falls, off Pilgrim Road, north of the bypass. It's a mix of nineties colonials and ranches on quarter-acre lots, mostly young families and some empty-nesters who've been there since it was built. Very quiet, lots of cul-de-sacs, sidewalks on both sides which I appreciate. We're walking distance to Lucia's elementary school and about a five-minute drive to the Village park where they do the fall fest and the farmers market on Saturdays from May through October. The county park system is also right there — Menomonee Park has a beach and trails, and we're about thirty minutes from Kettle Moraine. Demographically it's still pretty white and Midwestern, though it's gotten more diverse in the seven years we've been here. There's a small but growing Latino community — there's even a panadería that opened in a strip mall on Appleton Avenue two years ago.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: The four houses closest to us, yes. We do a block party every July and there's a group text for snow emergencies and lost dogs. Beyond that it's wave-from-the-driveway level.

follow_ups.question: What's the farmers market like?
follow_ups.response: Small but solid. We go almost every Saturday in season. There's a guy who sells sourdough that Lucia is obsessed with, and a flower vendor where Camila always picks up zinnias.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very safe. I let Lucia ride her bike to the end of the block and back. We leave the garage open during the day sometimes, which I shouldn't, but that's the level of trust. The biggest crime issue is occasional car break-ins when people leave them unlocked overnight.

follow_ups.question: Has that always been true, or has it shifted?
follow_ups.response: Always been true since we've been here. If anything, the village has added more crossing guards and slowed traffic on Pilgrim, so it feels safer for kids than when we moved in.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Mostly up. Great schools, low taxes for what you get, easy commute to downtown Milwaukee. The down is the lack of diversity and the cultural offerings — for live music or a good Ecuadorian restaurant we drive into the city. And the winters are long, no way around that.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever felt out of place there?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally. At a Village board meeting once when I raised a question about a sidewalk project, someone asked where I was 'originally from' in a way that wasn't curious. Mostly people are fine though.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just the three of us — me, Camila, and Lucia. We also have a beagle named Pancho and a betta fish that Lucia named Sparkle. My mom stays with us for stretches in February and again in July around Camila's birthday week, but those are visits, not residents.

follow_ups.question: Have you considered having more kids?
follow_ups.response: We're in the discussion phase. Camila wants one more, I'm on the fence — I'd want to be sure I can be present, and right now with the PE exam and the senior associate ramp, I'm honestly not.

follow_ups.question: Who handles what in the household?
follow_ups.response: We split it pretty evenly. I do all the cooking on weekends and Tuesdays, yard work, and finances. Camila does weeknight dinners, laundry, and most of the school logistics.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone's permanent. Just the three of us full-time.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My mom for a week or two at a time, maybe three times a year. My sister and her family come for long weekends a couple of times a year.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one. Everyone in the household is currently home.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays I'm up at 5:45, run or bike on the basement trainer for forty minutes, shower, make Lucia's lunch, and head to the office in Brookfield by 7:45. Three days a week I'm in the office; Tuesdays and Fridays I work from home unless I have a site visit. I usually have a community meeting one or two evenings a week — Village board, the Hispanic Collaborative, or a Habitat board call. Soccer is Wednesday nights at 8 from April through October, indoor at the Uihlein Soccer Park in winter. Thursdays I have a standing call with my PE study group. Saturday is family day — farmers market, library, errands. Sundays are mass with my mom maybe twice a month, then a big lunch, then I try to do PE prep for two or three hours in the afternoon.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wrap work?
follow_ups.response: Try to be done by 5:30 so I can do bath and bedtime with Lucia. I'm back on the laptop after she's down maybe two or three nights a week for an hour.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a hard 'off' day?
follow_ups.response: Saturdays I really try. Camila enforces it. No work email until Sunday afternoon.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm a senior associate civil engineer at a mid-sized engineering and architecture firm in Brookfield. We do municipal infrastructure, water and stormwater, transportation, and some institutional buildings — schools, libraries, community centers. My personal portfolio is mostly stormwater management and complete-streets projects for villages in southeast Wisconsin. I work standard hours, roughly 7:45 to 5:30, but I have flex on when and where. I'm responsible for design oversight on three to five projects at a time, leading public engagement, and mentoring two junior engineers.

follow_ups.question: What's a typical site visit look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually a couple of hours on a construction site walking with the contractor's superintendent and our resident engineer, checking conformance, then maybe a stop at the village engineer's office to debrief. I do those mostly on Wednesdays.

follow_ups.question: How much of your time is design versus management?
follow_ups.response: Now it's maybe 30 percent design and 70 percent management and client work. Three years ago it was the opposite.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I'm on the board of the Milwaukee Habitat for Humanity chapter — that's a quarterly board meeting and usually a Saturday build day each month from April to October. I also volunteer with SHPE Milwaukee, doing a STEM night at a Milwaukee public school once a month during the school year. And I help organize the Hispanic Heritage Month programming at the Menomonee Falls Public Library — that's a heavy lift in September and October, light the rest of the year.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep all that from becoming overwhelming?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, I don't always succeed. Camila has a rule — no more than three standing volunteer commitments at once — and I broke it last fall and paid for it. I'm trying to honor that rule this year.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Two big ones. First, I made senior associate in January, which means I'm in more business development meetings and fewer hands-on design sessions. Second, I started a structured PE exam study plan in March — ten hours a week, two weekday evenings and Sunday afternoon. The exam is in October, so this routine is locked in until then. I've also cut back on social commitments to make room.

follow_ups.question: How's the PE prep going?
follow_ups.response: Slower than I'd like. The geotech section is humbling. But my study group keeps me accountable.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Lucia is up around 7, breakfast — usually oatmeal or yogurt with berries. Camila walks her to school by 8:15. She's in kindergarten until 3:10. Mondays she has Spanish enrichment at the library until 4. Wednesdays she has a little kids soccer clinic at the YMCA. Thursdays she has Suzuki violin lessons — she's been doing those since she was four. Tuesdays and Fridays are unstructured — usually a playdate or backyard time. Dinner around 6, bath at 7, books and bed by 8.

follow_ups.question: Whose idea was the Suzuki violin?
follow_ups.response: Camila's. She did it as a kid. I was skeptical at first but Lucia loves it now.

follow_ups.question: How much screen time does she get?
follow_ups.response: Maybe an hour on weekdays, two on weekends. Bluey, Wild Kratts, occasionally an Encanto rewatch for the eight-hundredth time.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly routine and uneventful. I've been pulled over maybe four times in my adult life — three for speeding, one for a tail light. The most memorable was in 2014 in Waukesha, on a stretch of road I now know is heavily patrolled. The officer was professional, ran my license, gave me a written warning. I have a clean record. I've also worked with police on traffic-calming designs as part of my job, so I have a kind of professional relationship with the Menomonee Falls department.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about the police generally?
follow_ups.response: Complicated. I think most individual officers are decent people in a hard job. I also think the systems they operate in have real problems, especially around accountability. Both things can be true.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: In 2020 during the protests in Milwaukee after George Floyd, I went to one downtown with Camila. The MPD presence was heavy and tense. Nothing happened to us personally, but I'll never forget the feeling of being on Wisconsin Avenue with a line of officers in riot gear watching us.

follow_ups.question: Did that change anything for you?
follow_ups.response: It made me more attentive to how my Black friends and colleagues experience the same systems I encounter pretty benignly.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not in my immediate family. A cousin in New York was arrested for a DUI in 2018. Nobody has been incarcerated long-term. I've never been arrested.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: Every election. Presidential, midterm, primaries, Village board, school referenda, spring judicial races — I vote in all of them. Wisconsin's spring elections matter a lot and most people skip them. I usually vote early in person at the Village Hall.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide on the down-ballot races?
follow_ups.response: I read the local Milwaukee Journal Sentinel coverage, look at the Wisconsin Civic Engagement Project guides, and ask Priya — she's deeply plugged in. For judicial races I look at the Wisconsin State Bar evaluations.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd describe myself as a center-left Democrat with strong pragmatic streaks. On economics, I believe in robust public investment in infrastructure — obviously, given my job — and in a strong safety net, especially around healthcare and childcare. I think the ACA didn't go far enough and that we should have a public option, but I'm not a single-payer purist. On immigration, my views are shaped by my family's story; I support clear pathways to citizenship and I think the current asylum system is broken in ways that hurt both migrants and host communities. On climate, I'm probably most activated — I work in this field and I see municipalities making decisions today that will lock in flooding and heat exposure for decades. I'm a strong supporter of carbon pricing and federal investment in resilient infrastructure. Socially, I'm pretty liberal — marriage equality, reproductive rights, trans rights, the standard package. Where I'm probably more moderate than some of my friends is on policing — I think we need real accountability and reform but I'm skeptical of full defunding as a strategy. I also think the Democratic Party has a real problem talking to working-class voters of all races, including Latinos, and I'd love to see more focus on dignity-of-work framing.

follow_ups.question: Where did your political views come from?
follow_ups.response: A mix. My dad was a union guy in spirit even when his jobs weren't union, and he voted Democrat his whole life. My mom is more conservative, especially socially — she's pro-life and votes that way. I've been more shaped by my mom's commitment to community and my dad's economic populism than by any one party.

follow_ups.question: Are you a member of any political organizations?
follow_ups.response: Not formal party stuff. I'm on the email list for Voces de la Frontera and I donate annually to the Sierra Club and to MICAH.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more skeptical of national-level politics and more focused on local. Five years ago I spent a lot of time arguing about cable news topics; now I'd rather get a stormwater referendum passed in our village than dunk on a senator. I've also become more sympathetic to YIMBY-style housing arguments — I used to be more cautious about density but watching the housing affordability crisis up close, especially through Habitat, changed my mind. And I've gotten more impatient with purity politics on the left. We need to win elections to do anything.

follow_ups.question: What prompted the YIMBY shift?
follow_ups.response: Sitting through Village board meetings where neighbors fought a 12-unit townhouse project for two years. Eventually I just thought, this is irrational, and the people who'd live there are exactly the teachers and nurses I want in our community.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat to a lot, depending on the week. As a brown man in Wisconsin I navigate this stuff personally, though I want to be careful not to equate the Latino experience with the Black experience — they're related but not identical. The 2020 moment was genuinely formative for me. I read a lot — How to Be an Antiracist, The Sum of Us, Caste. I had hard conversations with my mom and with some white colleagues. At work, I pushed our firm to do real equity work on community engagement — translating materials, going to meetings in the actual neighborhoods instead of expecting people to come downtown at 6 PM on a Tuesday. So it's affected me practically, not just intellectually.

follow_ups.question: Has the energy on these issues changed since 2020?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it's cooled, and some of the backlash has been ugly. I think the actual work — at the local level, on policy — has continued even as the national conversation has receded. That's where I try to keep my focus.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core moral claim — that Black lives are devalued in American systems and that this has to change — is unimpeachable. The policy proposals are more contested and I have different opinions on different ones. I'm strongly in favor of independent civilian oversight, demilitarization, ending qualified immunity, and serious investment in mental health response. I'm less convinced by abolition framings as a near-term strategy, though I think they push the Overton window in useful ways. I also think the movement's emphasis on housing, healthcare, and education as racial justice issues is exactly right.

follow_ups.question: How do those issues show up in your work?
follow_ups.response: All the time. Stormwater investment maps almost perfectly onto historical redlining maps in Milwaukee. The neighborhoods most exposed to flooding are the ones that were systematically disinvested in. Designing infrastructure equitably is racial justice work whether anyone calls it that or not.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we're in a backlash period. The 2020 consensus that systemic racism is real and worth addressing has frayed, and there's a real political coalition working to undo even modest equity work in schools, in corporate America, and in government. At the same time, the demographic and cultural changes that prompted the original backlash aren't reversing. So I expect a couple of harder years and then, hopefully, a more durable settlement. Personally, I'm focused on what I can control — how my daughter understands her own heritage, how my firm engages communities, how I show up as a Latino professional in mostly white rooms.

follow_ups.question: How are you teaching Lucia about her heritage?
follow_ups.response: Spanish at home, music, food, video calls with family in Ecuador. We took her to the Mexican consulate's Día de los Muertos event last year. She has both flags in her bedroom and she knows where they are on a map.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: All of the above. I went to two protests in 2020, I've had a lot of conversations with family — some hard ones with my mom — and I've changed how I do my actual work. I've also donated to bail funds and to the ACLU of Wisconsin.

follow_ups.question: What was the hard conversation with your mom about?
follow_ups.response: She had absorbed a lot of anti-Black framing from Spanish-language media and from people at church. We've had several conversations. She's come some distance. Not all the way, but some.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed. Camila and my sister are basically where I am. My soccer crew is split — Diego is more progressive than me, Marcus is a moderate Republican and we've had to find ways to talk about it without fighting. My mom and my in-laws are more conservative on these questions, and we mostly agree to disagree at family dinners. My work friends are pretty uniformly progressive, which is its own bubble I try to be aware of.

follow_ups.question: How do you keep the friendship with Marcus working?
follow_ups.response: We focus on what we share — soccer, kids the same age, both of us care about our communities — and we go in pretty quick when we hit a real disagreement. He listens. So do I.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Generally good. I'm 39, six feet, around 180 pounds. I exercise five days a week, eat reasonably well. I have mild seasonal allergies — Wisconsin spring tree pollen is brutal — for which I take Zyrtec. I had ACL reconstruction on my right knee in 2008 from a soccer injury and it still aches in cold weather. I had a borderline-high LDL reading at my last physical and my PCP wants to see if diet changes bring it down before considering a statin.

follow_ups.question: Who's your primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Dr. Patel at Aurora Wauwatosa. I've been with her about five years.

follow_ups.question: How are you handling the cholesterol thing?
follow_ups.response: More oats, more fish, less red meat. Camila's on board so it's been easier than it would be solo.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: I genuinely love exercise, I have a spouse who's a healthcare worker and keeps me honest, and we have decent insurance through my job. Hard: long winters where outdoor activity drops off, sit-at-a-desk job, business lunches with clients, and stress eating during deadlines. The PE study schedule has made sleep harder, which is the underrated health input.

follow_ups.question: What's your sleep like normally?
follow_ups.response: Normally 7 to 7.5 hours. Right now I'm running on more like 6.5 and I can feel it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Two things. The cholesterol thing I mentioned, which came up at my October 2025 physical. And I tweaked my lower back in February doing snow-shoveling — saw a chiropractor and a PT for six weeks and it's resolved, but I'm now religious about lifting form. Otherwise, knock on wood, nothing major.

follow_ups.question: Did the back thing slow you down?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I missed about three weeks of soccer and had to skip a winter snow-shoeing weekend Camila and I had planned. Frustrating but minor.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Not in any serious way. The back thing took me out for a few weeks but I worked from home through it. Allergy season I'm less sharp in the mornings before the Zyrtec kicks in. Nothing that's threatened my ability to provide.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes — my dad's stroke and death in 2021 was the big one. He had a hemorrhagic stroke at 67 and was on a ventilator for four days before he passed. We were managing my mom's grief and her own blood pressure issues for a long time after. She's stable now, on lisinopril and statins, but it was a haul. My mother-in-law also had a breast cancer scare in 2023 — biopsy came back benign, but the waiting was terrible.

follow_ups.question: How are you and your mom doing with the grief now?
follow_ups.response: Better. Year three was harder than I expected — the freshness wore off and the permanence sank in. We talk about him a lot, which I think helps both of us.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have good employer-sponsored insurance and we live near major hospital systems, so access has been fine. The main pain points have been wait times for specialists — Lucia's pediatric dermatology referral took four months — and the byzantine billing. Camila's biopsy generated about a dozen separate bills from different entities and we had to dispute two of them. I haven't had to forgo care personally, but I've delayed routine things like dental cleanings when work got crazy.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about your insurance situation?
follow_ups.response: Lucky. I'm aware that most Americans have a worse experience than we do, and that bugs me as a policy matter.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Some. My mom is a big believer in agua de manzanilla for stomach issues, eucalipto rubs for colds, and various herbal teas. I grew up on those and I still default to them. We also do acupuncture occasionally — Camila found a practitioner in Wauwatosa after my back thing. I tried it once, found it helpful but didn't keep up. Not anti-alternative, but I lean evidence-based.

follow_ups.question: Does your mom give Lucia those remedies?
follow_ups.response: Always. We don't fight it. Manzanilla isn't going to hurt anybody.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I don't smoke and never have. I drink moderately — a beer or two after soccer, wine with dinner a few nights a week, more on social occasions. During the stretch after my dad died I was drinking more than I should have, maybe four or five nights a week with a couple of drinks each time. Camila and I had a conversation about it about six months in and I dialed it back. Now it's more like two or three nights a week, two drinks max.

follow_ups.question: Any other coping mechanisms?
follow_ups.response: Exercise, mostly. And cooking — I find chopping and prep meditative. I make a lot of ceviche when I'm stressed.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Not really. I took a short course of cyclobenzaprine for the back injury, maybe four or five doses total in February. I've tried edibles socially a couple of times — most recently at a friend's birthday in Denver last summer. Not a regular thing. No interest in anything stronger.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Through my employer's PPO plan. We pay about $480 a month in premiums for family coverage; my employer covers the rest. Deductible is $1,500 family, out-of-pocket max $6,000. We have an HSA we contribute to monthly. In a normal year we spend maybe $2,000 to $3,000 out of pocket all-in.

follow_ups.question: How does that compare to what your parents had?
follow_ups.response: Way better. My dad was on Medicaid for years and my mom was uninsured for stretches. Their experience of healthcare was constant rationing.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Strongly in favor. I'm up to date on everything — COVID boosters, annual flu shot, tetanus, HPV which I got in my twenties after the catch-up recommendation expanded. Lucia is fully on schedule per the CDC. Camila as a pediatric clinician is also fully vaccinated.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: The CDC, our pediatrician, my own PCP, Camila's clinical knowledge, and journalists I trust — Ed Yong's work, Katelyn Jetelina's Your Local Epidemiologist newsletter. I subscribe to that and read it every week.

follow_ups.question: Do you encounter vaccine skepticism in your circles?
follow_ups.response: Some, mostly from extended family. I share Katelyn's stuff when relevant. I don't argue with strangers online.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly good, with a layer of exhaustion. The promotion to senior associate has been gratifying and stressful in roughly equal measure. The PE prep is grinding. I'm in a good place with Camila and Lucia. I've had moments of feeling spread thin — particularly in January when the new role started, the PE plan kicked in, and my mom had a health scare all in the same three-week window. Overall though, I'd say a 7 out of 10 on a typical day, dipping to 5 on hard ones, hitting 9 on really good ones like Lucia's birthday or a great soccer game.

follow_ups.question: What does a really good day look like?
follow_ups.response: Cool morning run, productive few hours of work where I actually finish something instead of just attending meetings, lunch with Priya, bike ride with Lucia after school, Camila and I make ceviche together, in bed by 10.

follow_ups.question: What does a hard day look like?
follow_ups.response: Bad meeting where a client undercuts a community engagement decision I fought for, then home tired, snap at Camila about nothing, can't focus on PE prep, scroll my phone too late.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last November my firm lost a big municipal contract I'd been the relationship lead on for two years. The decision came down to politics on the client side, not our proposal, but it still felt like a personal failure. I took it hard — slept badly for a week, snapped at Lucia over something tiny, withdrew from Camila. She called it out on a Saturday morning and I just kind of broke down. We talked, I called my sister, I went for a long run, and by Monday I had some perspective back. But it stuck with me. I started seeing a therapist in December, partly because of that.

follow_ups.question: How's therapy going?
follow_ups.response: Useful. I see her every other week. She's helping me notice the pattern where I take work outcomes personally.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I'd say I have mild anxiety that's mostly situational and tied to work and family pressure. After my dad died I went through what I'd now call a depressive episode for about four months — low energy, lost interest in soccer, was hard to be around. I didn't get clinical help then; I should have. I'm in therapy now and managing well. No medication currently.

follow_ups.question: What helped you come out of that 2021 stretch?
follow_ups.response: Time, soccer when I forced myself back, Camila's patience, and Lucia. It's hard to stay in a hole when a two-year-old wants you to read Dragons Love Tacos for the eighth time.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Camila has been pretty steady. She has her own therapist and has for years, which I think is part of why she's so grounded. My mom has gone through real grief and some anxiety, manages it with church and family. My sister is fine, generally a low-anxiety person. Lucia is six and her main worry is whether we have enough strawberries.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Important but complicated. I was raised Catholic, baptized, first communion, confirmed. I went to Catholic mass every Sunday until I left for college. In my twenties I drifted; I had real frustrations with the Church on women's ordination, on LGBTQ inclusion, and on the abuse crisis. I came back partway when Lucia was born — we baptized her, and we go to mass at St. Mary's in Menomonee Falls maybe two Sundays a month, more during Advent and Lent. I'd call myself a culturally and ethically Catholic person who has serious institutional disagreements with the Church. The community, the sacraments, the social teaching — those are deeply mine. The hierarchy and many of its current positions are not. Father Esteban at St. Mary's is a good guy who knows how I feel and we have honest conversations about it.

follow_ups.question: Do you pray?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Not always formally. Before meals, on my morning run sometimes, when I'm worried about my mom. Less ritual, more conversation.

follow_ups.question: What about Camila?
follow_ups.response: She was raised Catholic too. She's roughly where I am — culturally yes, institutionally skeptical. We do the family rituals together.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Instagram daily, mostly for family stuff and following architects, civil engineering content, and food accounts. I have a Facebook account I check maybe weekly, mostly to stay in touch with extended family in Ecuador and to see updates from neighborhood groups and the Habitat chapter. I'm on LinkedIn pretty actively for work — that's where I follow industry stuff and post about projects. I have a Bluesky account I check a few times a week for civic and policy conversation; I left Twitter in 2023. No TikTok. I deleted Snapchat years ago.

follow_ups.question: How much total time on social per day?
follow_ups.response: Probably 30 to 45 minutes, mostly broken into short scrolls. I set screen time limits on Instagram.

follow_ups.question: Do you post yourself?
follow_ups.response: On Instagram, occasionally — soccer photos, projects I'm proud of, food. On LinkedIn, maybe once a month.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Not really for emotional support — I go to people directly. I did do a fundraiser on Facebook for the Ecuadorian Red Cross after the floods in 2023, and contributed to several GoFundMes for community members.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is up because of the PE exam and the senior associate ramp. My coping has gotten more deliberate — I started therapy, I'm more rigid about exercise, I've cut back on alcohol, and I've started a brief journaling practice three nights a week. Camila notices when I drift and tells me, which helps.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: My wife Camila and our daughter Lucia. Plus our dog Pancho. Just the three of us human-wise.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: Lucia is six — kindergartener, not a baby anymore, but small.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone's home.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Camila and I, equally.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Mortgage was the biggest — $2,150 PITI. Daycare and after-care for Lucia, about $1,100. Groceries around $900. Two car payments totaling $720. Utilities maybe $350. We also paid the first half of a kitchen backsplash project, about $1,800.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month was about $9,200 with the backsplash. A typical month is more like $7,400. The extras last month were the renovation and a flight for my mom to visit my sister.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. Bought in 2018 for $312,000, refinanced in 2021 to a 2.8% rate which we will hold onto until we're carried out. Current Zillow estimate is around $440,000.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Heating in January and February runs our gas bill up to $280 a month versus $60 in summer. Summer brings the soccer registration fees, camp for Lucia at $400 a week for two weeks, and our anniversary trip. December has Christmas spending, maybe $1,500 between gifts and travel to my sister's. Property taxes hit twice a year, January and July, about $3,200 each.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: Mostly from cash flow and our short-term savings. The backsplash we'd saved for specifically over six months. The summer camp we budget annually. We don't typically need to borrow for predictable bumps.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We save in several buckets. High-yield savings for emergency fund, currently sitting at about $32,000, roughly five months of essential expenses. 401(k) through my employer, I contribute 10% and they match 5%; current balance around $190,000. Roth IRAs for both of us, maxed annually. A 529 for Lucia at about $28,000. And the HSA. We're pretty disciplined.

follow_ups.question: How long did it take to build the emergency fund?
follow_ups.response: About four years post-2018. We started slow because the down payment had wiped us out.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Both. Beyond the standard buckets, we have a sinking fund for the Ecuador trip I want to do with Lucia — about $4,500 saved toward a $9,000 goal. And we're starting to think about whether we want to do a small addition on the house, which would be a longer horizon.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: Mortgage, principal balance about $228,000. Two car loans — Camila's CR-V at $14,000 left and my Civic at $7,000 left. No credit card debt; we pay in full monthly. Student loans I paid off in 2019 — I had about $34,000 from undergrad.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Honestly, not in the past year. We've been in a fortunate stretch. There have been moments earlier in our marriage — particularly 2019 when Lucia was born and Camila was on partial-paid leave — where things were tight, but not recently.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Civil engineer, senior associate. My main duties are: leading the design of municipal infrastructure projects, particularly stormwater systems, complete streets, and small public buildings; overseeing junior engineers and CAD technicians on those projects; serving as the primary client and community engagement contact for a handful of village and city clients; preparing and presenting public meetings, including bilingual outreach for projects in mixed-language neighborhoods; writing proposals and contributing to business development; ensuring compliance with Wisconsin DNR, DOT, and local code requirements; and reviewing construction-phase submittals and pay applications. I'm not yet a licensed Professional Engineer — I work under the seal of a PE colleague while I prep for the exam in October.

follow_ups.question: What's a current project you're proud of?
follow_ups.response: A green-infrastructure stormwater project in a flood-prone neighborhood in West Milwaukee that integrates a bioswale, a small public art installation by a local muralist, and pedestrian-scale lighting. Construction starts this fall.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No. Engineering at our firm is non-union. I'm a member of ASCE and SHPE as professional associations, but those aren't bargaining units.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: All 52. I took three weeks of vacation, but those count as paid weeks. No unpaid leave.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Usually 45 to 50. Sometimes 55 on a deadline week.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yes. Full week.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No, just the one. I've turned down small consulting work because of capacity.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: One.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: Gross monthly is about $9,580. After tax, 401(k), HSA, and benefits, my take-home is around $6,200.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Bi-weekly. 26 paychecks a year.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Camila grosses about $5,800 a month. So household gross is around $15,380 a month, $184,500 a year roughly.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, filed jointly for tax year 2025 in April. We use a CPA in Brookfield, Sandra Holloway — Camila's parents recommended her years ago.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: Nine years and four months. Benefits are solid — PPO health, dental, vision, four weeks PTO, two weeks sick, 401(k) with 5% match, HSA contribution, $1,500 annual professional development stipend, parental leave of eight weeks paid.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: Very good overall. My manager David is a principal who's been there 22 years; he's been a real mentor. I'm close with Priya and a few others on the engineering side. Some friction with one principal who's resistant to community engagement work, but manageable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Mostly predictable. I know my hours week to week. Flexibility is genuinely good — I can shift hours for a doctor's appointment or a school event without any drama. I work from home two days a week. The exception is bid deadlines and construction season, where evenings and a Saturday or two get eaten.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Daycare and after-care are expensive but we can afford them. The harder thing is the unexpected — sick days, snow days. Camila and I trade off who covers.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No. We have not been on any public benefits since I was a teenager when my family was on SNAP briefly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: Honestly hasn't happened in the past year. The leanest stretch in my adult life was 2010 through early 2012 when I was unemployed in engineering. I waited tables, did contract CAD work, lived with my parents, didn't go out. Nothing like that recently.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: We'd absorb it without thinking. The emergency fund covers it. That hasn't always been true — when we were first married, $400 would have been a credit-card moment. I don't take it for granted.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Grateful and a little anxious. Grateful because by any reasonable measure we're doing well — own our home, save consistently, no consumer debt, both of us employed with benefits, and we can afford the things that matter to us. Anxious because I'm aware of how thin the line is and how quickly things can shift. My family didn't have what we have, and I sometimes feel like I'm just one bad downturn away from being where they were. That's probably a first-gen thing as much as a financial reality.

follow_ups.question: What would change financially if you got the PE?
follow_ups.response: Probably $15,000 to $20,000 in base salary, plus my consulting potential opens up. The bigger thing is mobility — I can leave for a competitor or start something on my own if I want.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married. To Camila since June 2015.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
transcript.response: August 14, 1986.

transcript.question_text: Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Born in the U.S. — Queens, New York. My parents immigrated from Ecuador in 1982.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Queens, New York. Specifically Elmhurst Hospital.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: Yes — Ecuadorian-American.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: I usually mark 'other' and write in mestizo. On forms that force a single category I pick white, but that's not really how I think of myself.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering, UW-Milwaukee, 2009.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: Not formally enrolled in a degree program. I'm taking a PE prep course through a continuing-education provider, but that's not credit-bearing.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: Not in a degree program, no.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No, I have not served.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: Catholic, with the caveats we discussed earlier.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Democrat, moderately strongly. I'm a registered Democrat in Wisconsin, I vote D in nearly every race, and I donate to Democratic candidates and causes occasionally. I'm not a partisan in the sense that I'd defend any Democrat — there are state and local D's I've voted against in primaries — but at the general election level I'm reliably Democratic.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Democratic Party, clearly. The current Republican Party's positions on immigration, climate, voting rights, and most social issues are non-starters for me.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Near 27th and Lincoln, south side.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both. They were married my whole life.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My younger sister Marisol, and for about two years when I was 14 to 16, my tía Rosa from Ecuador stayed with us while she got established here.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: He finished the equivalent of high school in Ecuador, no college.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: She finished about three years of high school in Ecuador. She got her GED here in the U.S. when I was about twelve.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, basically my whole childhood.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She cleaned office buildings for a commercial cleaning company at night — vacuuming, trash, bathrooms, desk dusting on a four-floor rotation. During the day she did alterations and tailoring for neighbors out of our apartment. She was always working.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A commercial cleaning contractor that serviced downtown Milwaukee office towers — law firms, insurance companies. They cleaned offices overnight on contract.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, always.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: In Queens he was a baker at a commercial bakery — early mornings, mixing dough, running ovens. In Milwaukee he switched to hospital maintenance and custodial work at Aurora Sinai, eventually moving into a lead role on the night shift. His duties were facilities upkeep — repairs, cleaning, setup for events, light maintenance.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Aurora Sinai Medical Center, a hospital in Milwaukee. Healthcare. He worked in facilities for about 20 years until his stroke.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In five years I hope I have my PE, I'm leading a portfolio of large climate-resilient infrastructure projects in southeast Wisconsin, and maybe I've started or joined a smaller firm that does this work the way I think it should be done — community-first, art-integrated, sustainability-real-not-performative. I want Camila and me to have figured out whether we're having another kid. I want Lucia to be a curious, bilingual ten-year-old who's been to Ecuador at least twice. I want my mom to be healthy and close. I want to have taken Camila to the Pacific Northwest and to have hiked at least part of the Andes. And I want to still be playing soccer and to have not become so career-focused that I missed any of it. Mostly I want to stay grounded — like, do good work, raise a good kid, take care of my people, be present.

follow_ups.question: What scares you about that future?
follow_ups.response: Not getting the PE this fall. Burnout. Missing Lucia's childhood because of work. Climate stuff that affects our ability to live the way we live now.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family, first. Camila and Lucia and my mom and my sister. Then community — being someone the people around me can count on, whether at the firm, on the soccer field, at Habitat, at St. Mary's. Then craft — doing my engineering work in a way I'm proud of. Then the bigger arc — leaving the places I touch a little better, a little more inclusive, a little more sustainable than I found them. Those are the four, in that order.

summaries.demographer: Osvaldo Vargas is a 39-year-old first-generation Ecuadorian-American man (Q86, Q88), born in Queens in August 1986 to Ecuadorian immigrants who later relocated the family to Milwaukee; he holds a BS in Civil Engineering from UW-Milwaukee (Q90) and works as a senior associate civil engineer at a Brookfield firm (Q16, Q65). He is married since 2015 to Camila, a pediatric speech-language pathologist, and they have a six-year-old daughter (Q05, Q84); the household lives in an owned single-family home in a Menomonee Falls subdivision purchased in 2018 (Q58). His occupational trajectory shows clear upward mobility relative to his parents — a hospital custodian father and cleaner/seamstress mother with high-school-equivalent education (Q100-Q107) — placing him solidly in the professional-class second-generation Latino cohort. Household gross income is approximately $184,500/year with substantial savings, no consumer debt, and full employer-sponsored health coverage (Q40, Q61, Q63, Q74).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Osvaldo exhibits high planning orientation and strong self-control: he runs explicit cost-benefit spreadsheets on major decisions (Q03), maintains a multi-bucket savings architecture covering emergencies, retirement, 529, HSA, and a specific Ecuador-trip sinking fund (Q61, Q62), and treats large optional spending as pre-saved rather than financed (Q60). His time preferences are notably long — he accepted a roughly 50% pay cut in 2010 to align career with values, foregoing the Houston option for community-facing work (Q02). He shows mild loss aversion shaped by a first-generation scarcity background: even with strong objective finances he reports anxiety about being 'one bad downturn' from his parents' position (Q83). His behavior is strongly peer- and identity-influenced — soccer crew, SHPE network, and spouse exert meaningful corrective pressure (Q07, Q17), and he is highly responsive to professional validation (the lost November 2025 contract triggered a clear emotional drawdown, Q44).
summaries.political_scientist: Osvaldo is a high-information, high-participation center-left Democrat (Q23, Q24, Q95) who votes in every election including down-ballot judicial and school referenda, votes early in person at Village Hall, and uses curated sources — Journal Sentinel, WCEP guides, State Bar evaluations — for ballot decisions (Q23). His political identity is consistent but pragmatic: strongly aligned with Democrats on immigration, climate, voting rights, and social issues but more moderate on policing reform, sympathetic to YIMBY housing arguments, and skeptical of intra-coalition purity politics (Q24, Q25). Institutional trust is differentiated — high in local government, public agencies, and scientific institutions; lower in the national Republican Party and partial in the Catholic hierarchy (Q47, Q96). He combines deep civic embeddedness (Habitat board, SHPE, library programming, MICAH-adjacent advocacy) with bridging behavior across political difference, deliberately maintaining friendships with moderate Republicans in his soccer crew (Q07, Q30).
summaries.psychologist: Osvaldo presents as conscientious, agreeable, and moderately high in openness, with a service-oriented motivational structure (Q108, Q109) anchored in family, community, craft, and legacy. His emotional regulation is generally strong but vulnerable to over-commitment and identity-fusion with work outcomes, which he is actively working on in therapy initiated December 2025 (Q44, Q45). He shows healthy insight into his coping repertoire — exercise, cooking (especially ceviche when stressed), reduced alcohol, journaling, and direct conversation with his spouse and sister — and explicitly named a prior under-treated depressive episode after his father's 2021 death (Q38, Q45, Q50). Relationally he is securely attached: a confiding marriage with mutual corrective feedback, a sibling best-friendship, dense male friendships, and deliberate cross-generational mentoring. His self-concept integrates a clear first-generation Ecuadorian-American identity with professional and faith identities he holds with nuance and self-awareness (Q47, Q88, Q89).
